text.title: A Painful Case
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: Mr James Duffy, a solitary Dublin banker, meets and develops an intimate intellectual relationship with Mrs Sinico, a married woman. After she attempts to express physical affection, he ends the relationship. Four years later, he learns of her death by train accident and experiences a profound moral reckoning.

duffy.name: Mr James Duffy
duffy.description: A solitary Dublin banker living in Chapelizod who maintains strict control over his physical and mental life. He develops an intellectual relationship with Mrs Sinico but ends it when she expresses physical affection. After learning of her death, he experiences a profound moral crisis.
duffy.context: Early 20th century Dublin; represents a particular type of intellectual isolation and moral rigidity

data.physicalDescription: Face of brown tint of Dublin streets, long and rather large head, dry black hair, tawny moustache, harsh cheekbones, tawny eyebrows, unamiable mouth

mrs-sinico.name: Mrs Emily Sinico
mrs-sinico.description: A married woman with a daughter who meets Mr Duffy at a concert. She develops an intellectual and emotional relationship with him, seeking to open his nature. After Duffy ends their relationship, she descends into alcoholism and is killed by a train.
mrs-sinico.context: Wife of a sea captain; represents emotional sensitivity and the consequences of Duffy's moral rigidity

data.physicalDescription: Oval face with strongly marked features, very dark blue and steady eyes with defiant note, astrakhan jacket moulding a bosom of certain fullness

mary-sinico.name: Miss Mary Sinico
mary-sinico.description: The daughter of Mrs Sinico and Captain Sinico. She gives music lessons and attempts to help her mother with her drinking problem.
mary-sinico.context: Daughter of the Sinico household; represents family concern and propriety

data.physicalDescription: Young girl, daughter of Mrs Sinico

captain-sinico.name: Captain Sinico
captain-sinico.description: Husband of Mrs Sinico and father of Mary. He is captain of a mercantile boat plying between Dublin and Holland. He encourages Duffy's visits, mistakenly believing his daughter's hand is in question.
captain-sinico.context: Sea captain with Dutch ancestry; represents the absent husband and male indifference

data.physicalDescription: Captain of a mercantile boat; great-great-grandfather came from Leghorn

james-lennon.name: James Lennon
james-lennon.description: Driver of the train engine that strikes Mrs Sinico. He testifies at the inquest that he was in employment for fifteen years and responded to the guard's whistle.
james-lennon.context: Railway employee; represents the mechanical instrument of Mrs Sinico's death

p-dunne.name: P. Dunne
p-dunne.description: Railway porter who witnesses Mrs Sinico attempting to cross the lines. He testifies that he ran towards her and shouted but could not reach her before she was caught by the engine buffer.
p-dunne.context: Railway employee; represents the failed attempt to prevent the accident

sergeant-croly.name: Police Sergeant Croly
sergeant-croly.description: Police sergeant who arrives at the scene and finds Mrs Sinico on the platform. He has her body taken to the waiting-room.
sergeant-croly.context: Police officer; represents official response to the accident

constable-57e.name: Constable 57E
constable-57e.description: Police constable who corroborates Sergeant Croly's testimony at the inquest.

dr-halpin.name: Dr Halpin
dr-halpin.description: Assistant house surgeon of the City of Dublin Hospital who examines Mrs Sinico's body and testifies about her injuries. He concludes that death was probably due to shock and sudden heart failure.
dr-halpin.context: Medical professional; represents medical authority and explanation

h-b-patterson-finlay.name: Mr H. B. Patterson Finlay
h-b-patterson-finlay.description: Representative of the railway company who expresses regret at the accident and defends the company's precautions.
h-b-patterson-finlay.context: Railway company representative; represents institutional defense

deputy-coroner.name: Deputy Coroner
deputy-coroner.description: Official who presides over the inquest into Mrs Sinico's death. He expresses sympathy and urges the railway company to take preventive measures.
deputy-coroner.context: Legal official; represents official judgment and sympathy

landlady.name: Duffy's Landlady
landlady.description: Duffy's landlady who has a piano in her house. Duffy spends some of his evenings before her piano.
landlady.context: Landlady of Duffy's residence; represents domestic connection

pub-proprietor.name: Public-House Proprietor
pub-proprietor.description: Proprietor of the public-house at Chapelizod Bridge where Duffy goes after learning of Mrs Sinico's death. He serves Duffy obsequiously but does not venture to talk.
pub-proprietor.context: Publican; represents silent witness to Duffy's distress

waitress.name: Waitress at Eating-House
waitress.description: Waitress at the eating-house in George's Street where Duffy dines. She asks if his dinner is properly cooked when he stops eating.

chapelizod.name: Chapelizod
chapelizod.description: A suburb of Dublin where Mr Duffy lives in an old sombre house. He chooses it because he wishes to live as far as possible from the city and finds other suburbs mean, modern, and pretentious.
chapelizod.context: Suburb of Dublin; represents Duffy's chosen isolation from urban life
chapelizod.geography: Suburb of Dublin, on the Liffey River

chapelizod-house.name: Duffy's House in Chapelizod
chapelizod-house.description: An old sombre house where Mr Duffy lives. From his windows he can look into a disused distillery or upwards along the shallow river on which Dublin is built.
chapelizod-house.context: Duffy's private residence; represents his ordered, isolated life

duffy-bedroom.name: Duffy's Bedroom
duffy-bedroom.description: Duffy's uncarpeted room with lofty walls free from pictures. It contains carefully selected furniture: a black iron bedstead, iron washstand, four cane chairs, clothes-rack, coal-scuttle, fender and irons, and a square table with a double desk. A bookcase with white wooden shelves holds books arranged by bulk.
duffy-bedroom.context: Duffy's private bedroom; represents his austere, ordered life

rotunda-theatre.name: The Rotunda
rotunda-theatre.description: A theatre in Dublin where Mr Duffy meets Mrs Sinico and her daughter. The house is thinly peopled and silent, giving distressing prophecy of failure.
rotunda-theatre.context: Dublin theatre; represents chance meeting and cultural life

earlsfort-terrace.name: Earlsfort Terrace
earlsfort-terrace.description: A location in Dublin where Mr Duffy meets Mrs Sinico again at a concert a few weeks after their first meeting.
earlsfort-terrace.context: Dublin concert venue; represents cultural meeting place

sinico-house.name: The Sinico House
sinico-house.description: The house of Captain and Mrs Sinico where Mr Duffy visits. It is located outside Dublin. Duffy and Mrs Sinico spend evenings alone together in a cottage.
sinico-house.context: Sinico family residence; represents the space of Duffy and Mrs Sinico's relationship

baggot-street.name: Baggot Street
baggot-street.description: A street in Dublin where the private bank where Mr Duffy works as a cashier is located.

dan-burkes.name: Dan Burke's
dan-burkes.description: An establishment in Dublin where Mr Duffy takes his lunch at midday, consuming a bottle of lager beer and a small trayful of arrowroot biscuits.
dan-burkes.context: Dublin pub; represents Duffy's midday routine

george-street-eating-house.name: Eating-House in George's Street
george-street-eating-house.description: An eating-house in George's Street where Mr Duffy dines. He feels himself safe from the society of Dublin's gilded youth and appreciates the plain honesty of the bill of fare.
george-street-eating-house.context: Dublin restaurant; represents Duffy's dining routine and social avoidance

parkgate.name: Parkgate
parkgate.description: A location near Dublin where a cakeshop is located. Duffy and Mrs Sinico meet here to end their relationship.
parkgate.context: Dublin location; represents the place of separation

phoenix-park.name: Phoenix Park
phoenix-park.description: A large park in Dublin where Duffy and Mrs Sinico walk during their relationship and where Duffy walks alone after learning of her death. It contains Magazine Hill, gaunt trees, bleak alleys, and a wall.
phoenix-park.context: Dublin park; represents both intimacy and isolation

magazine-hill.name: Magazine Hill
magazine-hill.description: A hill in Phoenix Park where Duffy stands after learning of Mrs Sinico's death. From the crest he can see the river towards Dublin and human figures lying in the shadow of the Park wall.
magazine-hill.context: Location in Phoenix Park; represents Duffy's moment of moral reckoning

sydney-parade-station.name: Sydney Parade Station
sydney-parade-station.description: A railway station where Mrs Sinico is struck by a train and killed. She is attempting to cross the lines when she is hit by the engine of the ten o'clock slow train from Kingstown.
sydney-parade-station.context: Dublin railway station; represents the site of Mrs Sinico's death

city-of-dublin-hospital.name: City of Dublin Hospital
city-of-dublin-hospital.description: The hospital where Mrs Sinico's body is taken and where the inquest is held. Dr Halpin is an assistant house surgeon there.
city-of-dublin-hospital.context: Dublin hospital; represents medical authority and official response

inquest-venue.name: Inquest Venue
inquest-venue.description: The location where the Deputy Coroner holds the inquest on Mrs Sinico's body. Various witnesses testify about the circumstances of her death.
inquest-venue.context: Official legal venue; represents institutional judgment

chapelizod-bridge-pub.name: Public-House at Chapelizod Bridge
chapelizod-bridge-pub.description: A public-house at Chapelizod Bridge where Mr Duffy goes after learning of Mrs Sinico's death. He orders hot punch and sits observing the workingmen.
chapelizod-bridge-pub.context: Dublin pub; represents Duffy's refuge and reflection

dublin.name: Dublin
dublin.description: The city of Dublin, Ireland, where most of the story takes place. Duffy lives in Chapelizod to escape the city. The city is built on a shallow river.
dublin.context: Early 20th century Dublin; represents urban life and society

kingsbridge-station.name: Kingsbridge Station
kingsbridge-station.description: A railway station in Dublin from which a goods train departs. Duffy sees this train while standing on Magazine Hill and hears the engine's drone.
kingsbridge-station.context: Dublin railway station; represents mechanical fate

lucan-road.name: Lucan Road
lucan-road.description: A road visible from Duffy's window where lights appear in houses during the evening.

disused-distillery.name: Disused Distillery

disused-distillery.context: Industrial site; represents decay and abandonment

liffey-river.name: The Liffey River
liffey-river.description: The shallow river on which Dublin is built. Duffy can see it from his window and walks along it in the Park. It winds towards Dublin with lights burning redly and hospitably.
liffey-river.context: Dublin river; represents natural continuity and flow

irish-socialist-party.organizationalStructure: Divided into three sections, each with its own leader and garret

e01-room-description.description: Detailed description of Mr Duffy's austere bedroom in Chapelizod, including his carefully selected furniture, books, and writing materials arranged with meticulous order.

e02-duffy-character-description.description: Physical and psychological description of Mr Duffy, including his saturnine appearance, his aversion to disorder, his autobiographical habit, and his firm walking manner.

e03-duffy-routine.description: Description of Mr Duffy's daily routine: working as a bank cashier in Baggot Street, taking lunch at Dan Burke's, dining at an eating-house in George's Street, and spending evenings before his landlady's piano or roaming the city outskirts.

e04-duffy-isolation.description: Description of Mr Duffy's spiritual and social isolation: he has neither companions nor friends, no church nor creed, and lives an adventureless life despite theoretically being willing to rob his bank.

e05-rotunda-meeting.description: Mr Duffy meets Mrs Sinico and her daughter at the Rotunda theatre. Mrs Sinico remarks on the poor attendance, and Duffy engages her in conversation. He is struck by her intelligence and appearance, particularly her dark blue eyes and sensible demeanor.

e06-earlsfort-meeting.description: Mr Duffy meets Mrs Sinico again at a concert in Earlsfort Terrace a few weeks later. He becomes intimate with her while her daughter's attention is diverted. He learns her name is Mrs Sinico, that her husband is a sea captain plying between Dublin and Holland, and that they have one child.

e07-third-meeting.description: Mr Duffy meets Mrs Sinico a third time by accident and finds courage to make an appointment with her.

e08-house-visits.description: Mr Duffy begins visiting Mrs Sinico's house. He forces her to invite him openly rather than meeting stealthily. Captain Sinico encourages the visits, mistakenly believing Duffy's intentions concern his daughter. Duffy has many opportunities to enjoy Mrs Sinico's society while her husband is away and her daughter is giving music lessons.

e09-intellectual-sharing.description: Mr Duffy and Mrs Sinico develop an intellectual relationship. He lends her books and shares his ideas. She becomes his confessor. He tells her about his involvement with the Irish Socialist Party, his scorn for phrasemongers, and his belief that no social revolution will strike Dublin for centuries. She asks why he doesn't write out his thoughts.

e10-emotional-deepening.description: Mr Duffy and Mrs Sinico's relationship becomes emotionally intimate. They visit her cottage outside Dublin and spend evenings alone together. Their union transforms Duffy, wearing away rough edges of his character and emotionalizing his mental life. He speaks of the soul's incurable loneliness. Mrs Sinico catches his hand passionately and presses it to her cheek.

e11-disillusionment.description: Mr Duffy is very much surprised by Mrs Sinico's physical gesture. Her interpretation of his words about the soul's loneliness disillusiones him. He does not visit her for a week, then writes asking her to meet him.

e12-final-meeting.description: Mr Duffy and Mrs Sinico meet in a little cakeshop near Parkgate during cold autumn weather. They walk in the Park for nearly three hours and agree to break off their intercourse. Duffy says every bond is a bond to sorrow. When they leave the Park, Mrs Sinico trembles violently. Duffy bids her good-bye quickly and leaves her. A few days later he receives a parcel containing his books and music.

e13-four-years-pass.description: Four years pass. Mr Duffy returns to his even way of life. His room still bears witness to his orderliness. He adds new pieces of music and two volumes by Nietzsche to his shelves. He writes seldom in his sheaf of papers. He avoids concerts lest he meet Mrs Sinico. His father dies and the junior partner of the bank retires. He continues his routine of work and solitary dining.

e14-newspaper-discovery.description: While dining at the eating-house in George's Street, Mr Duffy's hand stops as he is about to eat. His eyes fix on a paragraph in the evening paper propped against the water-carafe. He reads it attentively, unable to eat. He pays his bill and leaves. He walks quickly through the November twilight, then slackens his pace. He reaches his house and reads the paragraph again by the failing light of the window, moving his lips as a priest does when reading prayers in secret.

e15-inquest-account.description: The full newspaper account of the inquest into Mrs Emily Sinico's death. She was killed at Sydney Parade Station when she was struck by the engine of the ten o'clock slow train from Kingstown while attempting to cross the lines. Witnesses testify about the circumstances. Dr Halpin concludes death was probably due to shock and sudden heart failure. Captain Sinico testifies that his wife had become intemperate in her habits about two years ago. Miss Mary Sinico testifies that her mother had been going out at night to buy spirits. The jury exonerates all parties.

e16-initial-revulsion.description: Mr Duffy raises his eyes from the paper and gazes out at the cheerless evening landscape. He is revolted by the account of her death and by the thought that he had ever spoken to her of what he held sacred. He judges her harshly, seeing her as unfit to live, without strength of purpose, an easy prey to habits. He questions whether he had deceived himself about her. The shock attacks his stomach, then his nerves. He puts on his overcoat and hat and goes out. He comes to the public-house at Chapelizod Bridge and orders a hot punch.

e17-public-house-reflection.description: Mr Duffy sits in the public-house, observing the workingmen discussing a gentleman's estate in County Kildare. He sits on his stool, gazing at them without seeing or hearing them. After they leave, he calls for another punch and sits a long time over it. As he sits there, living over his life with Mrs Sinico, he realizes she is dead, that she has ceased to exist, that she has become a memory. He begins to feel ill at ease and asks himself what else he could have done. He realizes how lonely her life must have been, sitting alone night after night. He understands that his life will be lonely too until he dies and becomes a memory.

e18-park-walk.description: After nine o'clock, Mr Duffy leaves the public-house and enters Phoenix Park. He walks under gaunt trees through the bleak alleys where he and Mrs Sinico had walked four years before. He feels her presence and questions why he withheld life from her and sentenced her to death. He feels his moral nature falling to pieces. He reaches Magazine Hill and sees human figures lying in the shadow of the Park wall. He feels outcast from life's feast, realizing he had denied her life and happiness. He sees a goods train winding out of Kingsbridge Station and hears the engine's drone reiterating her name. He turns back, the rhythm of the engine pounding in his ears. He halts under a tree and allows the rhythm to die away. He realizes he cannot feel her near him and waits in perfect silence. He feels that he is alone.

Formalist Reading.name: Formalist Reading
Formalist Reading.description: A formalist interpretation of 'A Painful Case' focusing on narrative structure, literary devices, symbolic patterns, and the formal properties of the text itself. This reading emphasizes how Joyce's careful construction of language, imagery, and narrative technique creates meaning through form rather than external reference.

theme-paralysis.name: Paralysis and Stasis
theme-paralysis.description: The formal repetition of Duffy's routines and the cyclical return to isolation demonstrate how the narrative structure itself enacts paralysis. The story moves from isolation to connection back to isolation, creating a closed formal loop.

theme-language-limitation.name: Language and Inexpressibility
theme-language-limitation.description: The gap between what can be articulated and what is felt drives the narrative. Duffy's intellectual discourse masks emotional incapacity; Mrs Sinico's physical gesture exceeds language. The formal tension between dialogue and action creates meaning.

theme-form-content-disjunction.name: Disjunction Between Form and Content
theme-form-content-disjunction.description: The meticulous formal ordering of Duffy's life (his room, routine, intellectual pursuits) contrasts sharply with the emotional chaos beneath. This formal-thematic tension is central to the story's meaning.

theme-narrative-irony.name: Narrative Irony and Unreliable Judgment
theme-narrative-irony.description: The narrator's formal presentation of events creates ironic distance. Duffy's self-justifications are formally undercut by the narrative structure, particularly in the final section where his moral certainty collapses.

sym-room-order.name: The Ordered Room
sym-room-order.description: Duffy's meticulously arranged bedroom functions as a formal symbol of intellectual control and emotional repression. The careful cataloguing of objects mirrors the narrative's own formal precision.

sym-train-engine.name: The Train Engine
sym-train-engine.description: The train that kills Mrs Sinico functions formally as the narrative's instrument of fate and as a sonic/rhythmic element that intrudes upon Duffy's consciousness. Its mechanical repetition echoes the story's formal patterns.

currentMeanings.description: Intrusion of external reality into consciousness
The sound of guilt and moral reckoning

sym-newspaper-text.name: The Newspaper Paragraph
sym-newspaper-text.description: The newspaper account functions formally as a textual interruption that shatters Duffy's narrative. Its formal presentation (the inquest testimony) contrasts with the intimate narrative that precedes it.

currentMeanings.description: The inadequacy of language to capture truth

sym-phoenix-park.name: Phoenix Park
sym-phoenix-park.description: The park functions formally as a liminal space where past and present, life and death, intersect. Its gaunt trees and bleak alleys create a formal landscape that mirrors Duffy's internal state.

symrel-room-paralysis.name: Room as Formal Enactment of Paralysis
symrel-room-paralysis.description: The ordered room symbolizes the paralysis theme through its formal properties: the careful arrangement of objects mirrors the narrative's circular structure, both returning to the same state.
symrel-room-paralysis.nature: The room's formal perfection enacts the story's thematic concern with stasis and the inability to change or escape established patterns.
symrel-room-paralysis.interpretation: The room's formal perfection enacts the story's thematic concern with stasis and the inability to change or escape established patterns.

symrel-train-language.name: Train Engine as Language Failure
symrel-train-language.description: The train's mechanical sound represents the failure of language to express or contain emotional truth, paralleling the theme of language limitation.
symrel-train-language.nature: The engine's drone 'reiterating her name' shows how mechanical repetition replaces meaningful communication, enacting the formal problem of linguistic inadequacy.
symrel-train-language.interpretation: The engine's drone 'reiterating her name' shows how mechanical repetition replaces meaningful communication, enacting the formal problem of linguistic inadequacy.

symrel-newspaper-irony.name: Newspaper as Narrative Irony
symrel-newspaper-irony.description: The newspaper's formal presentation of facts creates ironic distance from Duffy's subjective experience, embodying the narrative irony theme.
symrel-newspaper-irony.nature: The inquest testimony's objective tone contrasts with Duffy's emotional turmoil, formally demonstrating how external narrative can undercut internal certainty.
symrel-newspaper-irony.interpretation: The inquest testimony's objective tone contrasts with Duffy's emotional turmoil, formally demonstrating how external narrative can undercut internal certainty.

symrel-park-form-content.name: Park as Form-Content Disjunction
symrel-park-form-content.description: The park's formal beauty contrasts with its emotional desolation, embodying the disjunction between form and content.
symrel-park-form-content.nature: The park's gaunt trees and bleak alleys present a formally beautiful landscape that contains emotional emptiness, mirroring Duffy's own formal perfection masking inner void.
symrel-park-form-content.interpretation: The park's gaunt trees and bleak alleys present a formally beautiful landscape that contains emotional emptiness, mirroring Duffy's own formal perfection masking inner void.

narrator.name: Third-Person Omniscient with Ironic Distance
narrator.description: The narrator maintains formal omniscience while creating ironic distance from Duffy's perspective. The narrative voice is precise and controlled, mirroring Duffy's own linguistic precision, but this very precision creates ironic commentary on his self-deception.

reader.name: Formalist Reader
reader.description: The reader attends to the formal properties of the text: narrative structure, linguistic patterns, symbolic arrangements, and the relationship between form and meaning. The reader recognizes how the story's circular structure, repetitive patterns, and careful linguistic control enact its thematic concerns.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: Joyce constructs a formally precise narrative that uses linguistic control, symbolic patterning, and narrative structure to explore themes of paralysis and emotional limitation. The story's form—its careful ordering, its circular return, its ironic distance—becomes inseparable from its content.

e01-room-description.note: Establishes the formal principle of order that structures the entire narrative. The meticulous description creates the symbolic foundation for understanding Duffy's character and the story's formal concerns.

e02-duffy-character-description.note: Provides formal characterization through precise language and cataloguing. The description's style mirrors Duffy's own orderly nature, creating formal self-reflexivity.

e03-duffy-routine.note: Establishes the repetitive formal pattern that will structure the narrative. The routine's mechanical nature enacts the paralysis theme through form.

e04-duffy-isolation.note: Formalizes Duffy's spiritual state through language. The paradox of his theoretical willingness to rob the bank contrasts formally with his actual passivity.

e05-rotunda-meeting.note: Introduces the disruption of Duffy's formal order. The meeting's formal structure (theatre setting, conversation) begins to complicate the established pattern.

e06-earlsfort-meeting.note: Develops the formal pattern of repeated meetings. The gathering of information about Mrs Sinico creates narrative momentum against the established stasis.

e07-third-meeting.note: Brief transitional event that formalizes the shift from chance to intentional meetings. Its brevity contrasts with surrounding events.

e08-house-visits.note: Establishes a new formal pattern of regular visits. The misunderstanding about Mary creates ironic narrative distance from Duffy's perspective.

e09-intellectual-sharing.note: Central to the language-limitation theme. The dialogue form contrasts with what remains unspoken, creating formal tension between articulation and silence.

e10-emotional-deepening.note: The narrative reaches its formal and emotional climax. The shift from intellectual to emotional language marks the story's turning point. Mrs Sinico's gesture exceeds linguistic expression.

e11-disillusionment.note: The formal rupture point. Duffy's surprise at physical affection creates the narrative's central irony: his intellectual discourse masks emotional incapacity. The week of silence is formally significant.

e12-final-meeting.note: Formalizes the separation through the park setting and the agreement to break off. The return of books and music creates formal closure to the relationship.

e13-four-years-pass.note: Establishes the formal return to stasis. The addition of Nietzsche volumes and the continued routine demonstrate the circular structure. The passage of time is formally compressed.

e14-newspaper-discovery.note: The formal interruption that shatters the established pattern. The newspaper's intrusion into Duffy's meal creates a formal break in the narrative. The description of his reading (moving lips like a priest) is formally significant.

e15-inquest-account.note: The formal presentation of objective facts creates ironic contrast with subjective experience. The inquest testimony's formal structure (witnesses, evidence, verdict) contrasts with the intimate narrative preceding it.

e16-initial-revulsion.note: Duffy's moral judgment is formally presented as revulsion. The physical shock (stomach, nerves) demonstrates the inadequacy of his intellectual framework to contain emotional reality.

e17-public-house-reflection.note: The formal shift from revulsion to recognition. Duffy's realization of Mrs Sinico's loneliness mirrors his own, creating formal symmetry. The repetition of 'punch' and sitting creates rhythmic significance.

e18-park-walk.note: The formal and thematic climax. The return to the park creates circular closure. The train's drone and the final silence are formally crucial. The story ends not with resolution but with recognition of isolation, enacting the paralysis theme.

duffy.note: The protagonist whose formal properties (orderliness, linguistic precision, emotional control) structure the entire narrative.

mrs-sinico.note: Her physical gesture and subsequent death function formally as the narrative's central disruption and revelation. Her absence becomes formally present through the newspaper account and Duffy's memory.

mary-sinico.note: Functions formally as a narrative device (her presence enables Duffy and Mrs Sinico's meetings) rather than as a developed character.

captain-sinico.note: His misunderstanding about Duffy's intentions creates formal irony but remains peripheral to the central narrative.

duffy-bedroom.note: Functions as a symbolic space that enacts the formal principle of order. Its description establishes the story's formal aesthetic.

sinico-house.note: The cottage represents the space where formal order breaks down, where intellectual discourse becomes emotional.

phoenix-park.note: Functions formally as a liminal space where past and present intersect. Its gaunt trees and bleak alleys create a formal landscape that mirrors internal states.

sydney-parade-station.note: The site of Mrs Sinico's death functions formally as the narrative's external event that triggers internal reckoning.

george-street-eating-house.note: The setting where the newspaper interrupts Duffy's routine, creating formal disruption of established pattern.

chapelizod-bridge-pub.note: Functions as a formal space of transition where Duffy moves from revulsion to recognition.

rotunda-theatre.note: The initial meeting place whose 'thinly peopled' and 'silent' nature foreshadows the story's themes of isolation.

earlsfort-terrace.note: The concert setting where Duffy becomes 'intimate' with Mrs Sinico, marking the shift from chance to intentional meetings.

evening-paper.note: Functions formally as the textual interruption that shatters Duffy's narrative. Its objective discourse contrasts with subjective experience.

bookcase.note: Symbolic representation of Duffy's intellectual order. The arrangement 'according to bulk' demonstrates his formal precision.

black-iron-bedstead.note: Part of the room's formal description, contributing to the symbolic representation of order and control.

sheaf-of-papers.note: Represents Duffy's intellectual ambitions and his failure to articulate his thoughts, connecting to the language-limitation theme.

stout-hazel.note: Duffy's walking stick functions as a formal attribute of his character, part of his orderly presentation of self.

james-lennon.note: The train driver functions formally as an instrument of fate rather than as a developed character.

p-dunne.note: Railway porter whose testimony contributes to the formal structure of the inquest account.

sergeant-croly.note: Police officer whose testimony contributes to the objective formal presentation of facts.

constable-57e.note: Minor witness whose corroboration contributes to the formal structure of the inquest.

dr-halpin.note: Medical authority whose clinical assessment contrasts with emotional reality.

h-b-patterson-finlay.note: Railway representative whose formal testimony contributes to the inquest structure.

deputy-coroner.note: Authority figure whose formal role structures the inquest account.

landlady.note: Part of Duffy's routine, contributing to the formal pattern of his isolated life.

pub-proprietor.note: Functions formally as a witness to Duffy's emotional state, though he 'does not venture to talk.'

waitress.note: Minor character whose question about Duffy's dinner marks the moment of interruption.

abs-duffy-intellectual-companionship.note: The desire for intellectual companionship structures the narrative's first half. Its formal presence through absence (what Duffy seeks) drives the plot.

abs-duffy-emotional-connection.note: The central absential that creates narrative tension. Duffy's simultaneous desire for and rejection of emotional connection structures the story's formal irony.

abs-duffy-moral-purity.note: Duffy's need for moral purity functions formally as the principle that structures his rejection of Mrs Sinico. Its collapse in the final section creates the narrative's formal reversal.

abs-mrs-sinico-emotional-openness.note: Mrs Sinico's desire to open Duffy's nature creates formal tension between her expressiveness and his restraint.

abs-mrs-sinico-companionship.note: Her unfulfilled desire for companionship structures the narrative's tragedy. Its absence becomes formally present through the inquest account.

abs-duffy-redemption.note: The central absential of the final section. Duffy's search for moral redemption creates the narrative's formal climax. The story ends with the recognition that redemption is impossible, enacting the paralysis theme.

span_1.note: Overall story tension arc from isolation through connection to final recognition of paralysis.

span_2.note: Establishment of formal order and isolation. Low tension as the narrative establishes its baseline state.

span_3.note: Description of room creates formal foundation. Tension minimal as this is purely descriptive.

span_4.note: Furniture arrangement establishes the principle of order that structures the narrative.

span_6.note: Character description creates formal self-reflexivity through precise language.

span_9.note: Routine establishes the repetitive formal pattern. Tension increases as the narrative moves toward disruption.

span_12.note: Isolation and meeting. Tension increases as the established order begins to be disrupted.

span_13.note: Formal statement of Duffy's isolation. Tension remains low as this establishes the baseline.

span_16.note: First meeting introduces disruption. Tension increases as the narrative begins to move away from stasis.

span_19.note: Developing relationship. Tension increases significantly as the formal order is increasingly disrupted.

span_20.note: Second meeting establishes pattern of repeated encounters. Tension builds as intimacy develops.

span_26.note: Intellectual intimacy. Tension high as the formal contrast between discourse and feeling becomes apparent.

span_30.note: Emotional deepening. Tension reaches near-climax as the narrative approaches the rupture point.

span_34.note: Rupture and separation. Tension remains high through the formal breaking of the relationship.

span_35.note: Disillusionment. The formal rupture point where Duffy's intellectual framework fails.

span_37.note: Final meeting formalizes the separation. Tension remains high as the relationship formally ends.

span_40.note: Four years pass. Tension drops dramatically as the narrative returns to stasis, demonstrating the circular formal structure.

span_43.note: Revelation and moral reckoning. Tension increases sharply as the newspaper interrupts the established pattern.

span_44.note: Discovery of newspaper. Tension high as the formal interruption shatters Duffy's routine.

span_48.note: Inquest account. Tension sustained as objective facts contrast with subjective experience.

span_53.note: Initial revulsion. Tension high as Duffy's moral judgment is formally presented.

span_57.note: Public-house reflection. Tension reaches climax as Duffy moves from revulsion to recognition.

span_60.note: Park walk. Final tension peak as the narrative reaches its formal and thematic climax. The circular return to the park creates formal closure.
